patients.label: Patient 1: 57-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder and malignant catatonia

identity_evidence.quote: A 57-year-old woman with a prior diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder

attribution_limitations: Narrative lists echolalia early after gastrectomy at the previous hospital, but Table 1 records echolalia as absent before and after treatment at the study hospital.

The authors hypothesize that catatonic symptoms emerged after combined olanzapine 20 mg and haloperidol 5 mg and that the course may have involved both NMS and malignant catatonia; this is interpretation, not a stated confirmed cause.
Improvement began while guanfacine was added alongside high-dose lorazepam and olanzapine changes; the authors state the improvement may have other causes.
Mild hypotension and dizziness on Days 24-35 were managed by lowering lorazepam; the narrative does not attribute them to guanfacine or reduce guanfacine for this patient.

Several Patient 1 findings (Day 7 vital signs, Day 8 conversation and oral nutrition, Day 14 olanzapine start and IV lorazepam, Day 15-17 nutrition, Day 17 catheter removal) are reported in sentences following a day-marked sentence; their facts carry no time, and timeline events group them with the preceding day only as narrative sequence.

patients.label: Patient 2: 54-year-old woman, paliperidone-associated catatonia

identity_evidence.quote: A 54-year-old woman with no prior history of psychiatric illness

attribution_limitations: The authors state remission after guanfacine is likely related to guanfacine but may instead reflect discontinuation of paliperidone LAI.
The discussion proposes that catatonia developed after paliperidone LAI 150 mg with concurrent olanzapine 10 mg; this is the authors' interpretation of timing.
Muscle rigidity is first listed among catatonia criteria and then described as determined to be an extrapyramidal symptom.

The abstract reports dizziness and fatigue in one patient and hypotension and bradycardia in two others as side effects resolved by dose reduction; the per-patient narratives (Patients 2, 3, 4) reduce guanfacine for these findings but do not name the patients in that aggregate statement.

patients.label: Patient 3: 56-year-old man, catatonia after paliperidone LAI during COVID-19

identity_evidence.quote: A 56-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia

attribution_limitations: The authors suggest catatonia may have been exacerbated by decreased medication tolerability after COVID-19 and state that catatonia appeared after paliperidone LAI 150 mg; resolution may have been partly due to the paliperidone dose reduction as well as guanfacine.

The paliperidone dose reduction to 100 mg is described as occurring at the next scheduled injection, whereas the discussion says it occurred prior to clinical improvement; relative timing to guanfacine improvement is not given in days.

patients.label: Patient 4: 62-year-old man, catatonia after lithium and risperidone

identity_evidence.quote: A 62-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia

attribution_limitations: The narrative names lithium (close temporal association) as possibly contributory and risperidone 7 mg as the causative agent of catatonia; these attributions are the authors' judgments.
The admission laboratory evaluation states no organic etiology for catatonia was found, but it is documented at admission before catatonia developed.
Mild hypotension and bradycardia were noted after guanfacine titration to 6 mg and guanfacine was lowered to 4 mg, but the narrative does not explicitly assign the cause.

patients.label: Patient 5: 63-year-old man, catatonia after benzodiazepine discontinuation

identity_evidence.quote: A 63-year-old man with a history of multiple hospitalizations for schizoaffective disorder

attribution_limitations: The case narrative says benzodiazepines were tapered and discontinued, while the discussion describes abrupt discontinuation of benzodiazepines as associated with onset of catatonia.
Hyponatremia and drug-induced SIADH are described as findings suggesting these diagnoses; the specific causative drug and whether it was carbamazepine are not explicitly stated.

claims.text: A 54-year-old woman without prior psychiatric history was admitted with schizophrenia (hallucinations and delusions); whole-body CT, EEG and blood tests excluded organic causes. She received risperidone 4 mg with olanzapine 10 mg, then risperidone was replaced by paliperidone LAI 150 mg every four weeks, with an additional 100 mg dose one week later, and she was discharged home.

claims.text: A 63-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder was admitted for a depressive state (decreased motivation, fatigue) on risperidone LAI 25 mg/2 weeks, levomepromazine, valproate, carbamazepine, sertraline and long-term etizolam, nitrazepam and triazolam. Because of repeated falls, including one with major temporal artery bleeding, the benzodiazepines were tapered and discontinued.

claims.text: He then developed mutism, negativism, mannerisms, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing and echolalia and was diagnosed with catatonia; benzodiazepine withdrawal was considered a likely contributing factor. Risperidone LAI, levomepromazine and sertraline were stopped and brexpiprazole 1 mg was started without benefit; intramuscular diazepam 5 mg gave partial relief.

Remission was maintained on brexpiprazole 2 mg, quetiapine, guanfacine and lorazepam, and he was discharged home.
